propositions.text: The claimants are citizens of Burundi: a 57-year-old male, his 42-year-old spouse, and their three children aged 11, 9, and 6.
propositions.quote: The claimants are citizens of Burundi. XXX XXXXX (the male claimant) is 57 years old. His spouse, XXXX XXXXX (the female claimant), is 42 years old. Their three children are XXXX XXXX XXXX, 11 years old, XXXX XXXX XXXX, 9 years old, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, 6 years old.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal states the claimants are a Burundian family: a 57-year-old man, his 42-year-old wife, and their three young children.

propositions.text: The female claimant was appointed designated representative for her three minor daughters.
propositions.quote: The female claimant was appointed the designated representative for her three minor daughters.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal notes the female claimant is the designated representative for her three minor daughters.

propositions.text: The claimants arrived in Canada on April 9, 2007, and claimed refugee protection that day.
propositions.quote: The claimants arrived in Canada on April 9, 2007, and claimed refugee protection that day.

propositions.text: The claimants allege a well-founded fear of persecution due to membership in a particular social group and political opinion.
propositions.quote: They made the claim because they allege a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of their membership in a particular social group and their political opinion.

propositions.text: The claimants allege risk to life, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and danger of torture if returned.
propositions.quote: They are also claiming refugee protection as persons in need of protection because they allege that they would be subjected to a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, as well as to a danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal records the claimants' arrival in Canada and their allegations of persecution, risk to life, cruel treatment, and torture.

propositions.text: The male claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF) contains his allegations.
propositions.quote: In his Personal Information Form (PIF), the male claimant alleges the following.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal introduces the male claimant's allegations as set out in his PIF.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges he is an ethnic Tutsi born in northwest Burundi.
propositions.quote: He is an ethnic Tutsi, born in northwest Burundi.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges he is an ethnic Tutsi from northwest Burundi.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges that after a 1966 coup, southern Tutsis discriminated against northern Tutsis and Hutus.
propositions.quote: after that, Tutsis in the south discriminated against those in the north and, to a much greater extent, all Hutus in the country.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges post-1966 coup discrimination by southern Tutsis against northern Tutsis and Hutus.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges that in 1971, non-southern army officers were charged and convicted for an attempted coup.
propositions.quote: In 1971, non-southern army officers were charged and convicted for an attempted coup.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges non-southern army officers were charged and convicted for a 1971 coup attempt.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges that in 1972, Hutus were victims of genocide and hundreds of non-southern Tutsis were also killed.
propositions.quote: In 1972, Hutus were victims of a genocide, but hundreds of non-southern Tutsis were also killed.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges that in 1972, Hutus and non-southern Tutsis were killed in genocide.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges he joined the army in 1973, unaware of its involvement in genocide, as the army had stopped targeting Hutus at his school.
propositions.quote: He was not aware of the army's involvement in the genocide, especially since the army had stopped going after Hutus at his school in XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges he joined the army in 1973, unaware of its involvement in genocide.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges he studied in the USSR, was discriminated against for not being a southern Tutsi, but was promoted in 1993.
propositions.quote: After achieving the rank of XXXX, he was subjected to discrimination because he was not a southern Tutsi. He was nevertheless promoted to XXXX in 1993.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges discrimination in the army for not being a southern Tutsi, but was promoted in 1993.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges southern officers attempted coups in 1993, President Ndadaye was assassinated, and he opposed the rebels, later being arrested and detained for 21 months.
propositions.quote: He went to XXXX on XXXX, 1993, where he was arrested and detained for 21 months.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges he opposed 1993 coups, was arrested, and detained for 21 months after President Ndadaye's assassination.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges he was charged with President Ndadaye's murder, but the charge was withdrawn; later charged with desertion, received a conditional sentence, and appealed to the Supreme Court.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was charged with the murder of President Ndadaye, but that charge was eventually withdrawn. Eighteen months after leaving for XXXX, he was charged with deserting the army and received a conditional six-month sentence. That sentence was appealed, and the Supreme Court proceedings have not yet been completed.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges charges of murder and desertion, with the murder charge withdrawn and the desertion appeal still pending.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges that after returning to Burundi, he faced serious problems: a grenade attack, arrest, increased taxes, and a failed pardon application.
propositions.quote: In 1997, a grenade was thrown at his business. In 2001, he was arrested and detained for four hours. In 2003 or 2004, his taxes increased considerably. Finally, his application for a pardon was unsuccessful.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges facing attacks, arrest, increased taxes, and a failed pardon application after returning to Burundi.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges that in 2006, he held a press conference to explain his innocence, seek a pardon, press the Supreme Court, and clarify his position on the coup.
propositions.quote: to explain that he had no role in the events of XXXX, 1993; to obtain a pardon; to press the Supreme Court to process his case; and to explain his position with respect to the coup.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges he took advantage of a political change to act.
propositions.quote: The male claimant took advantage of a change in the political environment to XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges he held a 2006 press conference to explain his innocence and seek legal remedies, using a political change as an opportunity.

propositions.text: The male claimant alleges that after the press conference, he received threats and feared for his family's lives, prompting their flight to Canada.
propositions.quote: After the press conference, the male claimant received numerous threats, to the point that he realized that his and his family's lives were at risk. That is why he left his country and claimed refugee protection in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges threats after a press conference led him to fear for his family's lives and seek refugee protection in Canada.

propositions.text: The male claimant's wife and children base their claims on his claim.
propositions.quote: The male claimant's wife, XXXX XXXX, and his children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, base their claim on that of their husband and father.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant's wife and children base their refugee claims on his claim.

propositions.text: The Minister alleges the male claimant was a Burundian army member from 1976 to 1993, promoted to XXXX.
propositions.quote: The Minister alleges that the male claimant was a member of the Burundian army from 1976 [sic] to 1993 and that he had been promoted to the rank of XXXX.

propositions.text: The Minister alleges the Burundian army committed human and international rights violations and the male claimant could have participated or been complicit in crimes against humanity or acts contrary to the UN.
propositions.quote: He also alleges that the Burundian army committed human and international rights violations and that the male claimant could have participated in or been complicit in crimes against humanity or acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the male claimant should be excluded under articles 1F(a) and (c) of the Convention.
propositions.quote: He is therefore of the opinion that the male claimant should be excluded under articles 1F(a) and (c) of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister alleges the male claimant was a senior army member possibly complicit in crimes, and should be excluded under Convention articles 1F(a) and (c).

propositions.text: The panel determines the male claimant is not a refugee or a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The panel determines that the male claimant, XXX XXXX, is not a refugee or a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the male claimant is not a refugee or a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The panel finds the female claimants are Convention refugees.
propositions.quote: the female claimants, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are Convention refugees.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the female claimants are Convention refugees.

propositions.text: The claimants have valid Burundian passports and other documents, so their identities are established.
propositions.quote: The claimants have valid identity documents, namely, passports issued by the Burundian authorities and several other documents. Their identities have therefore been established.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the claimants' identities are established by valid Burundian passports and other documents.

propositions.text: The male claimant testified at length with no contradictions, answered spontaneously, and much of his testimony was corroborated by documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The male claimant testified at length. His testimony contained no contradictions. He answered spontaneously and without hesitation. Moreover, much of his testimony was corroborated by an abundant amount of documentary evidence.

propositions.text: The panel did not accept all of the male claimant's statements.
propositions.quote: However, as will be mentioned later on, the panel did not accept all of his statements.

propositions.text: The female claimant testified briefly and her testimony was credible.
propositions.quote: The female claimant XXXX XXXX testified briefly, and her testimony was credible.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the male claimant's testimony mostly consistent and corroborated, but did not accept all his statements; the female claimant's brief testimony was credible.

propositions.text: Upon arrival in Canada on April 9, 2007, the male claimant answered questions about his military career to an immigration officer.
propositions.quote: Upon his arrival in Canada on April 9, 2007, the male claimant answered the questions of an immigration officer who questioned him, among other things, about his military career.

propositions.text: The male claimant addressed his military career in his PIF and added details during testimony.
propositions.quote: The male claimant also addressed this topic in his response to question 31 of the PIF, and he added some details when he testified.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant discussed his military career with an immigration officer, in his PIF, and during testimony.

propositions.text: The male claimant joined the army in 1973 at age 20, trained in the USSR for four years, and was promoted regularly.
propositions.quote: The male claimant joined the army in XXXX 1973, at the age of 20, at the invitation of the chief of staff at the time. He then began four years of training in the USSR. Up to the rank of XXXX, the male claimant, like his colleagues, was promoted regularly: he became a XXXX after six months, a XXXX XXXX XXXX after a year, and XXXX XXXX after two years.

propositions.text: He returned to Burundi in 1977, was promoted in 1978, and became a XXXX in 1983.
propositions.quote: He returned to Burundi in 1977 and was promoted to XXXX in XXXX 1978. Finally, he became a XXXX in XXXX 1983.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant joined the army in 1973, trained in the USSR, and received regular promotions, returning to Burundi in 1977 and advancing further.

propositions.text: The male claimant held various military positions from 1979 to 1993, including time in the USSR and promotions.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was a XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1979 and a XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1980. After a six-month stay in the USSR, from the end of 1982 to early 1983, the male claimant had XXXX XXXX XXXX. He returned to the USSR from 1987 to 1990. At the time, he was a XXXX-XXXX. Upon his return to the USSR, the male claimant was promoted to XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He then XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXX. This was an XXXX-XXXX XXXX XXXX, the male claimant's specialty. After a failed coup in XXXX 1993, in which the male claimant was not involved, he was transferred to XXXX XXXX, where he had the same duties.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant held various military roles, trained in the USSR, received promotions, and was transferred after a failed 1993 coup he was not involved in.

propositions.text: The male claimant stated he did not advance as quickly as southern Tutsis due to being a Tutsi from the northeast and had to protest for fairness.
propositions.quote: The male claimant stated that as a Tutsi from the northeast, he did not advance in his career as quickly as the southern Tutsis and that he had to protest to have this injustice corrected.

propositions.text: He was a XXXX - XXXX XXXX in 1990.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, he was a XXXX - XXXX XXXX in 1990.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant said his career advanced slowly due to his ethnicity, requiring protest, but he reached a senior rank by 1990.

propositions.text: In 1993, UPRONA lost elections to FRODEBU, a primarily Hutu party, leading to resistance and coup attempts by the army.
propositions.quote: In the presidential elections on June 1, 1993, and the parliamentary elections on June 29, 1993, the UPRONA party, which had led Burundi since 1965, lost to FRODEBU, a primarily Hutu party.3 Part of the Burundian army resisted the change and assisted with a first coup attempt on July 3, 1993.

propositions.text: On October 21, 1993, a coup attempt resulted in the assassination of President Ndadaye and others.
propositions.quote: On October 21, 1993, during another coup attempt, the newly elected president, Melchior Ndadaye was assassinated along with some ministers and parliamentarians.

propositions.text: The male claimant left Burundi in this context in 1993 and went to another country.
propositions.quote: It was in this context that the male claimant left Burundi on XXXX, 1993, and went to XXXX (now called the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX).

paragraphs.summary: The 1993 elections led to unrest, coup attempts, and the president's assassination, prompting the male claimant to leave Burundi.

propositions.text: The male claimant's testimony about his role in the October 1993 events and his forced stay is largely corroborated by documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The male claimant's testimony about his role in the events on October 21 and 22, 1993, and his forced stay in XXXX is largely corroborated by the documentary evidence.

propositions.text: The first and eleventh battalions were behind the coup; the male claimant went to XXXX at 1:00 a.m. on October 21, 1993, for a specific purpose.
propositions.quote: In short, the first and eleventh battalions were behind the coup. The male claimant, who XXXX XXXX XXXX, went to XXXX at around 1:00 a.m. on October 21, 1993, in order to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: The male claimant encountered obstacles and was unable to complete his intended actions during the coup events.
propositions.quote: Unfortunately, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, where XXXX XXXX was conducting operations. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who were to go to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the male claimant's account of the October 1993 events and his forced stay credible and corroborated by documents, detailing his actions and obstacles faced.

propositions.text: The male claimant stated a specific fact about his actions or identity during the events.
propositions.quote: The male claimant stated that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He stated that his name was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant made a statement about his actions or identity during the events.

propositions.text: The panel finds the male claimant's statement plausible and that he acted as described.
propositions.quote: The panel is of the opinion that this statement is plausible and that the male claimant XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

propositions.text: The male claimant discussed certain actions and submitted supporting evidence, including accounts and a DVD.
propositions.quote: The male claimant talked XXXX XXXX. Note that he XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.4 The male claimant also XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006, and XXXX XXXX for this is on file.5 He submitted four accounts of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.6 He also submitted the DVD XXXX XXXX,7 and the panel notes that approximately XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: The panel notes the content of the DVD and other evidence submitted by the male claimant.
propositions.quote: He also submitted the DVD XXXX XXXX,7 and the panel notes that approximately XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the male claimant's statement plausible, noting his actions and the supporting evidence, including accounts and a DVD.

propositions.text: The panel notes the male claimant's involvement or knowledge of the events on October 1993.
propositions.quote: The panel notes that the male claimant XXXX XXXX of the XXXX on XXXX, 1993.

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes the male claimant's involvement or knowledge regarding the October 1993 events.

propositions.text: On October 21, 1993, a council announced the coup's success and claimed the army and police had risen against the government.
propositions.quote: At 9:00 p.m. on October 21, 1993, a national public safety council broadcast the message that the coup had succeeded and that the entire army and police force had risen against the government.

propositions.text: On October 22, the coup was condemned by the international community and Burundian civil society.
propositions.quote: On October 22, the international community and Burundian civil society condemned the coup, to the extent that on October 23, Colonel Bikomagu read a news release on the radio and on television announcing that some parts of the armed forces had attempted a coup, but that the military command had ensured that constitutional legality would return.

paragraphs.summary: The coup was initially announced as successful, but was condemned by the international community and Burundian civil society the next day.

propositions.text: The male claimant fled Burundi at 10:00 a.m. on October 1993 to distance himself from the coup attempt.
propositions.quote: In the meantime, the male claimant fled Burundi at 10:00 a.m. on XXXX, 1993, to distance himself, according to him, from the coup attempt.

propositions.text: He turned himself in to authorities, was placed under house arrest, then transferred and imprisoned.
propositions.quote: He turned himself in to XXXX authorities and was placed under house arrest. From XXXX, he was transferred to XXXX, and on XXXX, 1993, he was transferred to XXXX and imprisoned.

propositions.text: He was detained with two others, including a cousin, for 21 months, all having left Burundi with help from a specific group.
propositions.quote: By coincidence, XXXX XXXX, XXXX of the coup attempt on July 3, 1993, and one XXXX XXXX coup on October 21, 1993, was also in Bukavu, as was his cousin XXXX, a XXXX XXXX. The documentation9 indicates that they left Burundi with help from the XXXX XXXX XXXX. The male claimant was detained in XXXX with these two individuals for 21 months.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant fled Burundi to distance himself from the coup, surrendered to authorities, and was detained with two others for 21 months.

propositions.text: The male claimant was detained at the Burundian government's request for extradition on charges of complicity in the president's assassination.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was detained at the request of the Burundian government, which had requested his extradition for complicity in the assassination of President Ndadaye.

propositions.text: Only the male claimant requested to be returned to Burundi to face charges, making this request in 1993.
propositions.quote: Only the male claimant requested that he be returned to Burundi to face the charges. He made this request on XXXX, 1993.

propositions.text: A list of letters he sent to authorities for repatriation is found in a weekly newspaper article.
propositions.quote: The list of letters that he sent to both XXXX and Burundian authorities in order to be repatriated to Burundi can be found in the article in the weekly newspaper XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant was detained for extradition on assassination charges, requested to return to Burundi, and sent letters to authorities seeking repatriation.

propositions.text: A UN Special Rapporteur wrote a report in 1994 about the male claimant's case, stating he wished to return and was detained illegally as a political prisoner.
propositions.quote: On XXXX, 1994, XXXX XXXX, Special Rapporteur for XXXX with the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, wrote a report specifically concerning the male claimant's case.12 He stated in particular that the male claimant wished to be returned to his country and concluded that the male claimant was being detained illegally and was a political prisoner.

propositions.text: Despite the report, the male claimant continued to be held at the request of the Burundian government until 1995.
propositions.quote: Despite this report, the male claimant continued to be held at the request of the Government of Burundi until XXXX, 1995.

paragraphs.summary: A UN report found the male claimant was illegally detained as a political prisoner, but he remained in custody until 1995.

propositions.text: The charge of attempt on the life of a head of state was withdrawn in 1995, but the male claimant was charged with desertion 18 months after incarceration began.
propositions.quote: The charge [translation] "of attempt on the life of a head of state" was withdrawn according to a letter from the Burundian minister of justice dated XXXX, 1995,13 but according to the male claimant, he was charged with desertion in XXXX 1995, that is, 18 months after his incarceration began.

paragraphs.summary: The assassination charge was withdrawn in 1995, but the male claimant was then charged with desertion 18 months after incarceration began.

propositions.text: The male claimant's lengthy detention constituted persecution.
propositions.quote: There is no doubt that the male claimant's lengthy detention in XXXX constituted persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds that the male claimant's lengthy detention was persecution.

propositions.text: Upon return to Burundi in 1995, court martial proceedings for desertion began; he was convicted and sentenced to six months' imprisonment in 1996.
propositions.quote: Upon his return to Burundi in XXXX 1995, court martial proceedings for desertion began. On XXXX, 1996, the male claimant was convicted of desertion and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment.

propositions.text: In 1999, the sentence was upheld but suspended; the matter is still being appealed.
propositions.quote: On XXXX, 1999, this sentence was upheld, but was suspended.15 This matter is still being appealed.

paragraphs.summary: After returning to Burundi, the male claimant was convicted of desertion, sentenced, and the sentence was later suspended; the appeal is ongoing.

propositions.text: The male claimant did not rejoin the army after 1995, lived with his brother, and opened a business in 1997.
propositions.quote: The male claimant did not seek to rejoin the army upon his return to Burundi in XXXX 1995. He lived with his brother until 1997, when he opened a XXXX.

propositions.text: He experienced several problems: a grenade attack in 1997, threats in 2000, brief detention in 2001, administrative problems from 2002-2004, and serious problems after 2006.
propositions.quote: At that time, he started having a number of problems. In XXXX 1997, someone threw a grenade into his business, fortunately causing little damage. In 2000, a colonel threatened officers who frequented his XXXX. In 2001, he was arrested and detained for four hours. From 2002 to 2004, he experienced administrative problems. But it was following the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006, that his problems became very serious.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant did not rejoin the army, opened a business, and faced escalating problems, including attacks, threats, and administrative issues, especially after 2006.

propositions.text: The male claimant explained he returned to Burundi to face accusers but misjudged the power structure, as coup supporters remained in power.
propositions.quote: The male claimant explained that he had returned to Burundi to face his accusers, but stated that that he had been mistaken about the power structure and that several supporters of the coup on October 21, 1993, were still in power and had even been promoted.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant returned to Burundi to face accusers but realized coup supporters were still in power and promoted.

propositions.text: The 1999 court martial decision was never legally served on the male claimant; his lawyers advised against requesting it.
propositions.quote: The 1999 court martial decision was never legally served on him. The male claimant's lawyers had advised him not to request it.

propositions.text: With political change in 2006, the male claimant sought to relaunch his case, requesting proper service of the decision and starting the appeal period.
propositions.quote: Since the political situation changed in 2006 and there was a new government and a new minister of justice, the male claimant felt it was a good time to relaunch his case. He requested that the 1999 decision be properly served on him, and the time frame for the appeal began from the moment it was served.

propositions.text: He decided to publicly reopen his case to have witnesses heard, rebuild his reputation, and state he was not involved in the conspiracy.
propositions.quote: It is in this context of political change and a new judicial remedy that the male claimant decided to publicly reopen his case. He wanted the right to have witnesses heard in his case, a right that had previously been denied. But, in particular, he wanted to rebuild his reputation, to testify about what he knew about the attempted coup on October 21, 1993, and to state publicly that he had never been involved in the conspiracy.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant, after political changes in 2006, sought to relaunch his case, have witnesses heard, and publicly clear his name regarding the coup.

propositions.text: The DVD of XXXX 16 shows the male claimant spoke freely and provocatively, naming soldiers involved in the coup who had been promoted.
propositions.quote: The DVD of XXXX 16 confirms that the male claimant talked with some freedom and even with a hint of provocation, naming soldiers involved in the coup who had been promoted.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the male claimant spoke freely and provocatively at the event, naming soldiers involved in the coup.

propositions.text: The male claimant likely miscalculated the risks he was taking by speaking out.
propositions.quote: it seems that the male claimant perhaps miscalculated the risks that he was taking.

propositions.text: After the conference, the male claimant received frequent anonymous threatening calls, including to his home phone answered by the female claimant.
propositions.quote: After the conference, the male claimant received a series of threatening calls on his cellphone. Some calls were even made to his fixed-line telephone, which the female claimant answered.

propositions.text: He was called a traitor, accused of being a FRODEBU member and a perpetrator of genocide.
propositions.quote: He was called a traitor. He was accused of being a member of FRODEBU and a perpetrator of genocide.

propositions.text: These anonymous calls were made frequently after the press conference.
propositions.quote: These anonymous calls were made frequently after the press conference.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the male claimant received frequent anonymous threats after the conference, including accusations and calls to his home answered by his wife.

propositions.text: In XXXX 2007, an anonymous caller referenced a murdered friend, prompting the male claimant to seek a US visa.
propositions.quote: Because of that threat, the male claimant decided to apply for a visa for the United States.

propositions.text: On XXXX, 2007, his car was vandalized and a threatening message referencing his family was left.
propositions.quote: someone punctured his tires, broke a window and the rear-view mirror, and left a message: [translation] "Remember that you have a wife and children".

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds that threats escalated to references to murder and vandalism, prompting the male claimant to seek a US visa.

propositions.text: A friend provided trustworthy soldiers to help the male claimant cross the border, knowing it would be difficult for him.
propositions.quote: a friend provided him with trustworthy soldiers to help him.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds a friend arranged for trustworthy soldiers to help the male claimant cross the border.

propositions.text: The claimants come from a country where 250,000 people have been killed since 1993.
propositions.quote: The claimants come from a country where 250,000 people have been killed since 1993.

propositions.text: There is a serious possibility the male claimant or his family would be attacked under the cover of generalized violence.
propositions.quote: there is a serious possibility, as the male claimant stated at the hearing, that he or his family would be attacked under the cover of generalized violence.

propositions.text: The economic power remains with the Tutsis, especially those from Bururi, whom the male claimant targeted in his accusations.
propositions.quote: The economic power still belongs to the Tutsis, especially those from Bururi, those whom the male claimant targeted in his accusations.

propositions.text: The male claimant's fear is well founded by reason of his political opinion, as defined in Ward.
propositions.quote: His fear is well founded by reason of his political opinion. Ward18 defines political opinion as any opinion on any matter in which the machinery of state, government and policy may be engaged. This is the case for the male claimant.

propositions.text: The family's fear is based on their membership in a particular social group (the family) and is also well founded.
propositions.quote: As for his family, which was directly targeted by the threats, their fear is based on their membership in a particular social group, the family. Their fear is also well founded.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the claimants face a serious risk of attack due to political opinion and social group, and their fears are well founded.

propositions.text: Given the reputation and political connections of those the male claimant accused, the claimants cannot expect adequate state protection or internal refuge in Burundi.
propositions.quote: the claimants cannot expect to receive adequate state protection or find refuge in the small country of Burundi.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the claimants cannot expect state protection or internal refuge in Burundi due to the accused's reputation and connections.

propositions.text: The Minister intervened to seek exclusion of the male claimant from protection under the Act, but not for the other claimants.
propositions.quote: The Minister intervened to have the male claimant, XXX XXXX, excluded from the protection that could be granted to him under the Act. A similar request was not made for the other claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal notes the Minister seeks exclusion only of the male claimant from protection under the Act.

propositions.text: Sections 96 and 97 of the Act define "refugee" and "person in need of protection"; section 98 excludes persons under sections E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention.
propositions.quote: Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act19 (the Act) define the terms "refugee" and "person in need of protection". Section 98 of the Act reads as follows: 98. A person referred to in section E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal sets out the statutory provisions defining refugee status and exclusion under the Act and the Refugee Convention.

propositions.text: Sections E and F of the Convention are incorporated into the Act; section F is relevant here and lists grounds for exclusion from protection.
propositions.quote: Sections E and F of the Convention have been incorporated into the Act. In this case, section F of article 1 of the Convention is relevant. It reads as follows: F. The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (a) he has committed a crime against peace, a war crime, or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crimes; (b) he has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee; (c) he has been guilty of acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal explains section F of Article 1 of the Convention, which lists grounds for exclusion from refugee protection.

propositions.text: Section F requires serious reasons for considering the crimes or acts specified were committed.
propositions.quote: As section F indicates, there must be serious reasons for considering that the crimes mentioned were committed or that the acts specified were carried out.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal states that section F requires serious reasons for considering the specified crimes or acts were committed.

propositions.text: The Minister bears the burden to prove the male claimant falls within the excluded category.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the Minister to prove that the male claimant falls within the category of excluded persons.

propositions.text: The Minister does not allege the male claimant directly committed crimes against humanity, but claims his position makes him an accomplice to regime crimes from 1973-1993.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the Minister did not claim that the male claimant himself had directly committed crimes against humanity. However, he claimed that because of the position that he held, he must be considered an accomplice in crimes committed by the regime in power from 1973 to 1993.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal notes the Minister must prove exclusion and alleges the male claimant is an accomplice due to his position, not direct acts.

propositions.text: Federal Court jurisprudence establishes that complicity requires personal and knowing participation or association with principal actors, with a shared common purpose and knowledge.
propositions.quote: Complicity rests on the existence of a shared common purpose and the knowledge that all of the parties may have of it: Ramirez; Moreno.

propositions.text: Mere membership in an organization that sometimes commits international offences is not normally sufficient for accomplice liability, unless the organization is principally directed to a brutal purpose.
propositions.quote: Those cases have established that mere membership in an organization which from time to time commits international offences is not normally sufficient to bring one into the category of an accomplice. At the same time, if the organization is principally directed to a limited, brutal purpose, such as a secret police activity, mere membership may indeed meet the requirements of personal and knowing participation.

propositions.text: Physical presence plus other factors may qualify as personal and knowing participation; bystanders or those with no intrinsic connection are not accomplices.
propositions.quote: Physical presence together with other factors may however qualify as a personal and knowing participation. As I understand the jurisprudence, it is that a person who is a member of the persecuting group and who has knowledge that activities are being committed by the group and who neither takes steps to prevent them from occurring (if he has the power to do so) nor disengages himself from the group at the earliest opportunity (consistent with safety for himself) but who lends his active support to the group will be considered to be an accomplice.

propositions.text: A shared common purpose exists where a member with knowledge of group crimes does not prevent or disengage but lends active support; this applies to ongoing, not isolated, offences.
propositions.quote: A shared common purpose will be considered to exist. I note that the situation envisaged by this jurisprudence is not one in which isolated incidents of international offences have occurred but where the commission of such offences is a continuous and regular part of the operation.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal cites Federal Court jurisprudence on complicity, requiring knowing participation, association, and active support in ongoing group crimes.

propositions.text: The male claimant served in the Burundian army from 1973 to 1993, which was dominated by Tutsis and committed serious human rights violations.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was a member of the Burundian army for 20 years, from 1973 to 1993. Numerous documents entered on the record show the army's complete domination by the Tutsi ethnic group during that period (and before) and the extremely serious human rights violations of which the army was guilty.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the male claimant served in a Tutsi-dominated army guilty of serious human rights violations from 1973 to 1993.

propositions.text: Events before 1973, including Tutsi dominance and Hutu victimization, are relevant context but not attributable to the male claimant.
propositions.quote: It is important to mention the events that happened before the male claimant joined the army in 1973, although what happened before 1973 cannot be held against him.

propositions.text: The Minority Rights Group International report summarizes that Tutsis, though a minority, dominated politics, army, civil service, education, and economy, with Hutus as main victims.
propositions.quote: the Tutsi have dominated politics, the army, the civil service, education and the economy; and up to the massacres of late 1993, the Hutu were by far the most numerous victims of ethnic-political violence.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal notes pre-1973 Tutsi dominance and Hutu victimization as context, citing a Minority Rights Group report, but does not attribute pre-1973 events to the claimant.

propositions.text: In 1965, a failed coup led to violent repression, killing the Hutu political elite and 2,500–5,000 people, ending Hutu political involvement for years.
propositions.quote: In 1965, a failed coup was violently repressed. The entire Hutu political elite was killed, which ended all Hutu political involvement for many years,26 and between 2,500 and 5,000 people died.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds that a failed 1965 coup led to mass killings of Hutus and ended their political involvement for years.

propositions.text: In 1972, another coup attempt led to the massacre of 100,000–200,000 Hutus, exile of 300,000, and near-total exclusion of Hutus from the army; no one was prosecuted.
propositions.quote: In 1972, another attempted coup was followed by the massacre of 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus and the exile of another 300,000. There were almost no Hutus left in the army. No one was prosecuted for this genocide.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the 1972 coup attempt led to mass Hutu killings, exile, and exclusion from the army, with no prosecutions.

propositions.text: From 1976 to 1987, the army remained powerful and Tutsi-dominated, with increased political prisoners and continued Hutu discrimination under successive Tutsi leaders.
propositions.quote: the army remained a major force. From 1984 to 1987, the human rights situation seriously deteriorated, with a considerable increase in the number of political prisoners. Pierre Buyoya, another southern Tutsi, came to power in September 1987, following a coup. The army continued to be dominated by the Tutsi-Hima elite (from the south), and the Hutus continued to be discriminated against and prosecuted.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the army stayed Tutsi-dominated and powerful, with worsening human rights and Hutu discrimination from 1976 to 1987.

propositions.text: The massacre of 100,000–200,000 Hutus in 1972 is corroborated by many documents in the record.
propositions.quote: The preceding events, specifically, of course, the massacre of 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus in 1972, are corroborated by many of the documents entered on the record.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds documentary corroboration for the 1972 massacre of 100,000–200,000 Hutus.

propositions.text: In 1988, the army was 99.7% Tutsi; after Hutu gangs killed Tutsis, the army massacred about 20,000 Hutus, most uninvolved, and 60,000 fled to Rwanda.
propositions.quote: In 1988, the Burundian army was almost entirely made up of Tutsis, who constituted 99.7% of the force.30 In August of that year, Hutu gangs massacred hundreds of Tutsis in the communes of Ntega and Marangara, in northern Burundi. The army re-established order, and in the following week, massacred approximately 20,000 Hutus, most of whom were not involved in the incidents. In addition, 60,000 Hutus fled to Rwanda.

propositions.text: The government admitted 5,000 deaths but did not take responsibility.
propositions.quote: The government admitted that 5,000 people had died, but did not take responsibility.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the 1988 army, almost all Tutsi, massacred about 20,000 Hutus after Hutu attacks, with 60,000 fleeing and no government responsibility.

propositions.text: Reyntjens describes the 1988 army response as indiscriminate massacre, using helicopters and mass executions, with women and children among victims; estimates up to 20,000 killed and 60,000 refugees.
propositions.quote: When the army intervened on August 17, it used the "steamroller" system, which had proven successful in 1972. Since the Tutsis had fled to neighbouring communes, the army shot at anything that moved. Helicopters were used for massive strafing and for launching incendiary grenades. According to an Amnesty International report, the soldiers' conduct proves "that their orders were not only to put an end to the disorder, but also to carry out mass executions of members of the Hutu community.... The troops were engaged ... in a repression of the entire Hutu civilian population aimed at punishing them and killing them, rather than at restoring order."

paragraphs.summary: Reyntjens describes the 1988 army response as an indiscriminate massacre of Hutus, with up to 20,000 killed and 60,000 refugees.

propositions.text: The facts about the August 1988 massacre are reported in other documents on the record.
propositions.quote: The facts relating to this massacre in August 1988 are reported in other documents entered on the record.

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes that the August 1988 massacre's facts are documented elsewhere in the record.

propositions.text: Buyoya, under international pressure, integrated Hutus into institutions, but the army resisted, leading to November 1991 events.
propositions.quote: Buyoya implemented significant changes and began to integrate Hutus into public institutions. However, the army resisted the change. Buyoya's message did not go over well in the military establishments, which is reflected in the events of November 1991.

paragraphs.summary: Buyoya's reforms integrating Hutus faced army resistance, which contributed to the November 1991 events.

propositions.text: On November 23, 1991, Hutu militants attacked police and military posts; the army's retaliation killed over 1,000 people, with the government admitting 500 deaths.
propositions.quote: The army's retaliation caused the deaths of more than 1,000 people, according to the various reports. The government admitted that 500 people died.

paragraphs.summary: The November 1991 army retaliation killed over 1,000 people, though the government admitted to 500 deaths.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity over many years, based on credible, uncontradicted international human rights reports.
propositions.quote: This documentary evidence leaves no doubt that the Burundian army committed, over numerous years, crimes against humanity.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds credible evidence that the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity over many years.

propositions.text: Mugesera v. Canada defines crime against humanity as requiring four elements: proscribed act, widespread/systematic attack, attack on civilians/group, knowledge of attack.
propositions.quote: a criminal act rises to the level of a crime against humanity when four elements are made out: 1. An enumerated proscribed act was committed...

paragraphs.summary: Mugesera v. Canada sets out the four elements required to establish a crime against humanity.

propositions.text: Murder is a proscribed act, and mass killings constitute a systematic attack, meeting the first two criteria for crimes against humanity.
propositions.quote: Murder is clearly a proscribed act and meets the first criterion. When the victims are in the thousands, it must be concluded that the attack is necessarily a systematic attack at the least.

propositions.text: The attacks were directed against the Hutu civilian population, meeting the third criterion.
propositions.quote: The third criterion requires that the attack be directed against a civilian population or an identified group; the documentary evidence shows that the Hutu civilian population was the victim of attacks by the army for years.

propositions.text: The Burundian army was aware of the context of the attack, meeting the fourth criterion.
propositions.quote: Finally, the person, that is, the Burundian army, was aware of the context of the attack. That also goes without saying.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds all four criteria for crimes against humanity are met regarding the Burundian army's actions.

propositions.text: The panel concludes the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity against Hutu civilians in 1965, 1972, 1988, and 1991.
propositions.quote: the panel therefore concludes that in 1965, 1972, 1988 and 1991, the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity against the Hutu civilian population.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity against Hutu civilians in 1965, 1972, 1988, and 1991.

propositions.text: The Minister did not allege the Burundian army was solely for a brutal purpose; it had other functions.
propositions.quote: the Minister did not allege that the Burundian army was an organization directed toward a limited and brutal purpose. In fact, it certainly had other functions.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister did not claim the Burundian army was solely a brutal organization; it had other roles.

propositions.text: The Minister did not allege the male claimant personally participated in massacres, but alleged complicity by association as an army member.
propositions.quote: The Minister also did not allege that the male claimant had participated personally in any massacres. Rather, he alleged that it was as a member of the army that he was complicit in crimes against humanity committed by the Burundian army.

propositions.text: The male claimant argued he was unaware of the army's crimes and later dissociated himself from it.
propositions.quote: The male claimant primarily argued that he was not aware of the crimes committed by the Burundian army and that, ultimately, he dissociated himself from it.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister alleged the male claimant was complicit by association, while the claimant argued lack of knowledge and later dissociation.

propositions.text: The panel finds confusion in the claimant's dissociation argument; he left due to a coup, not past army crimes, and was a member during those crimes.
propositions.quote: The male claimant might have dissociated himself from the army in 1993, but he allegedly dissociated himself because of those who had attempted the coup. His dissociation had nothing to do with the crimes committed by the army previously, when the male claimant was not only a member of the army, but also a member of XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant's dissociation was unrelated to the army's past crimes, as he was a member during those times.

propositions.text: The panel finds the claimant's claim of ignorance about army crimes not credible, as it is contradicted by his own PIF and other evidence.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that this statement is not credible. First, it is contradicted in his own PIF and in XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant's claim of ignorance about army crimes not credible, based on his own statements and evidence.

propositions.text: The claimant's PIF shows he was aware of massacres in 1965 and 1972, making ignorance implausible when he joined the army in 1973.
propositions.quote: This could not have been unknown, even by a young man of 20. As for the 1972 genocide, during which 100,000 to 200,000 people were killed, in part by the army, it is impossible that the male claimant did not know this fact at the time he joined the army.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds it implausible the claimant was unaware of the 1965 and 1972 massacres when joining the army in 1973.

propositions.text: The claimant's PIF acknowledges ongoing segregation and elimination of Hutus, showing awareness of the situation.
propositions.quote: Of course, the Hutus continued to be subjected to the most segregation, when they were not simply physically eliminated.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's PIF shows he was aware of Hutu segregation and elimination.

propositions.text: Some northern Tutsis held high army positions, including the chief of staff who helped the claimant become a soldier.
propositions.quote: some northern Tutsis held high-ranking positions. For example, the chief of staff who helped the male claimant become a soldier was from the north.

paragraphs.summary: Some northern Tutsis, including the chief of staff who helped the claimant, held high army positions.

propositions.text: The claimant's PIF states the army supported authoritarian regimes and coups, and calling it 'the great silent one' does not mean members were unaware.
propositions.quote: the male claimant called the army "la grande muette" [the great silent one], implying that army members did not speak, but that does not mean that they did not know anything.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's PIF shows the army supported regimes and coups, and silence does not imply ignorance among members.

propositions.text: In a 2006 press release, the claimant described being a powerless witness to the 1972 tragedy, showing awareness of mass killings.
propositions.quote: I was a powerless witness to this tragedy.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's 2006 press release shows he was aware of the 1972 mass killings.

propositions.text: The panel concludes the claimant must have known about the army's role in the 1965 and 1972 massacres when joining in 1973.
propositions.quote: the male claimant must have had a good idea of the army's role in the massacres in 1965 and 1972 when he joined the army in 1973.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes the claimant knew about the army's role in the 1965 and 1972 massacres when he joined.

propositions.text: The panel does not believe the claimant only heard rumours about the 1988 massacre, given his rank and position.
propositions.quote: The panel cannot believe that the male claimant knew nothing else, when he was already a XXXX-XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds it implausible the claimant only heard rumours about the 1988 massacre, given his position.

propositions.text: It is impossible the claimant, given his rank and location, knew little about the 1991 massacre, especially since the government admitted 500 deaths.
propositions.quote: It is impossible that the male claimant, who XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX and who had the rank XXXX, knew very little about this, especially since the government had admitted that 500 people had died.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds it impossible the claimant knew little about the 1991 massacre, given his rank and location.

propositions.text: The panel concludes the claimant was aware of the Burundian army's crimes against humanity while a member.
propositions.quote: the panel concludes that the male claimant was aware of the crimes against humanity committed by the Burundian army when he was a member.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes the claimant was aware of the army's crimes against humanity during his membership.

propositions.text: Complicity exists when one participates in an organization knowing it commits crimes against humanity and fails to stop or dissociate.
propositions.quote: there is complicity when there is "participation in an organization knowing it commits crimes against humanity, when combined with a failure to stop the crimes or disassociate oneself".

propositions.text: It is uncertain if the male claimant had enough influence to oppose the army's actions.
propositions.quote: It is not certain that the male claimant had enough influence to oppose the army's actions.

propositions.text: Regardless, the male claimant did not try to dissociate himself from the army.
propositions.quote: Regardless, he did not try to dissociate himself.

propositions.text: The male claimant stated only one colleague resigned and suffered economic hardship due to an order preventing re-employment without army authorization.
propositions.quote: The male claimant stated that he knew only one colleague who had resigned, and that person suffered economic hardship as a result because of an order preventing him from being hired without the army's authorization.

propositions.text: These problems did not affect the male claimant's safety and are not a valid reason to maintain association with the army.
propositions.quote: The panel is of the opinion that these problems did not affect his safety and could not be a valid reason for the male claimant to maintain his association with the army.

propositions.text: The male claimant could have left the army well before 1993.
propositions.quote: The panel is therefore of the opinion that the male claimant could have left the army well before 1993.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the male claimant did not dissociate from the army, could have left earlier, and hardship was not a valid reason to stay.

propositions.text: The male claimant had a very XXXX XXXX within the army.
propositions.quote: the male claimant had a very XXXX XXXX within the army.

propositions.text: Leadership positions entail more moral responsibility for organizational crimes; continued leadership with knowledge may be considered complicity.
propositions.quote: Those in leadership positions must bear more moral responsibility for crimes committed by their organizations than non-leaders.

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes the male claimant's significant army role and cites case law on greater responsibility for leaders in criminal organizations.

propositions.text: There are serious reasons to consider the male claimant committed a crime against humanity and must be excluded from protection under the Act.
propositions.quote: the panel is of the opinion that there are serious reasons for considering that the male claimant committed a crime against humanity and must be excluded from the protection that can be granted under the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds serious reasons to believe the male claimant committed a crime against humanity and must be excluded from protection.

propositions.text: The male claimant is a person referred to in article 1F(a) of the Convention.
propositions.quote: the panel determines that the male claimant, XXX XXXX, is a person referred to in article 1F(a) of the Convention.

propositions.text: As required by section 98 of the Act, the male claimant cannot be considered a refugee or a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Consequently, as required by section 98 of the Act, the male claimant cannot be considered a refugee or a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the male claimant excluded under article 1F(a) and section 98, so he cannot be considered a refugee or protected person.

propositions.text: The female claimants have established a serious possibility of persecution based on membership in a particular social group.
propositions.quote: they have satisfactorily discharged their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on one of the grounds set out in the Convention, that is, their membership in a particular social group.

propositions.text: The female claimants are Convention refugees in accordance with section 96 of the Act.
propositions.quote: Consequently, they are Convention refugees in accordance with section 96 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the female claimants established a serious possibility of persecution and declares them Convention refugees under section 96.
